clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP2C1, encoding a Golgi calcium/manganese pump (SPCA1)
Presents in early adulthood with recurrent flaccid vesicles, erosions, and macerated fissured plaques in the flexures (axillae, groin, neck, inframammary folds)
Lesions have a characteristic macerated appearance with painful longitudinal 'ripped-fabric' fissures
Friction, sweating, heat, and secondary infection are major aggravating factors
Unlike pemphigus it is not autoimmune; direct immunofluorescence is negative
Histology shows widespread suprabasal acantholysis giving a 'dilapidated brick wall' appearance
Secondary bacterial, candidal, or herpetic infection frequently drives flares and malodour
reference.pathophysiology: Hailey-Hailey disease is caused by loss-of-function variants in ATP2C1, encoding SPCA1, a pump that transports calcium and manganese into the Golgi apparatus of keratinocytes. Disturbed intracellular calcium homeostasis impairs the processing and trafficking of proteins needed for desmosomal adhesion, weakening keratinocyte cohesion. The resulting acantholysis is most pronounced in flexural skin subjected to heat, sweat, and friction, which further stress the fragile epidermis. The defect is partial and mosaic in effect, which is why lesions are localised to intertriginous sites rather than generalised.
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing extensive suprabasal acantholysis ('dilapidated brick wall')
Bacterial, fungal, and viral swabs during flares to identify superinfection
Family history assessment for dominant inheritance
redFlags: Sudden painful vesicular flare suggesting herpes simplex superinfection
Spreading cellulitis or systemic features from bacterial superinfection
A persistent, non-healing, or indurated plaque raising concern for squamous carcinoma within chronic lesions
reference.prognosis: It is a chronic relapsing condition with a benign course that does not affect life expectancy, but recurrent flexural erosions can substantially impair quality of life; symptoms often improve in later life and some patients respond well to measures reducing friction and infection.
pitfalls: Diagnosing recurrent intertrigo or candidiasis and missing the underlying genodermatosis
Failing to look for and treat secondary herpetic or bacterial infection during flares
Confusing it with autoimmune pemphigus and initiating inappropriate immunosuppression
Overlooking rare squamous change in longstanding lesions
